extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political history/constitutional theory (readers of Machiavelli and histories of Florence)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical principles for evaluating the stability and good constitution of republics: causes of constitutional change, institutional checks (executive, legislative, judicial), taxation rules, factional dynamics, and political conduct that preserve or undermine liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent changes in republics caused by oppression or licentiousness
rubrics_metrics.description: “All republics, especially such as are not well constituted, undergo frequent changes in their laws and manner of government; and this is not owing to the nature either of liberty or of subjection in general, as many think, but to downright oppression on one hand, or unbridled licentiousness on the other.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Real liberty and true obedience tend to preserve constancy in government; where the constitution is good the laws govern and prevent both oppression and licence. Anti-pattern: regimes that allow either concentrated oppression or unrestrained licence will see rapid and damaging constitutional change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty as a specious pretence
rubrics_metrics.description: “The name of liberty is often nothing more than a specious pretence, made use of both by the instruments of licentiousness... and by the promoters of slavery, who generally are the nobles.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of rhetoric invoking 'liberty' as a justification for factional self-interest. Warning: both popular demagogues and oligarchs may employ the language of liberty to advance opposite agendas that undermine genuine constitutional balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a constitutional magistrate to mediate nobles and commons
rubrics_metrics.description: When some wise, good, and powerful citizen has sufficient authority in the commonwealth to make such laws as may extinguish all jealousies betwixt the nobility and the people... that state may properly be called free, and its constitution looked upon as firm and permanent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: constitutionalize an executive or mediating office empowered to moderate conflicts between elites and commons. Institutionalized mediation reduces dependence on the personal virtue of individuals and produces more durable freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of executive power with constitutional checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Such a magistrate, possessed of the whole executive power, with a negative to defend it, and if the commons have the negative upon the purse and the laws, and the inquest of grievances, that executive power can hardly be ill used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design principle: pair a strong executive (able to act decisively) with robust counter‑majoritarian checks (commons' veto on purse/laws, inquest of grievances). This combination constrains abuse while preserving effective government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying solely on individual virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Both [nobility and commons] must be upheld by the spirit and fortune of one man alone, who yet may either be suddenly taken off by death, or overpowered by adversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: constitutional arrangements that function only while a particular leader is alive or fortunate are fragile. Prefer institutional safeguards so the state does not collapse if a single leader dies or falls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of independent judiciary under factional government
rubrics_metrics.description: “There can never be an independent judicial power: all parties are either courting, or threatening, or persecuting the judges.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for judicial health: judges must be insulated from factional appointment/pressure. Example failure mode: courts where presiding judges follow factional allegiance and are removed or retained for partisan advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assembly- or senate-management of executive power breeds factions and poor foreign policy
rubrics_metrics.description: When a popular assembly or a senate have the management of the executive power, disputes for ever arise concerning every step in foreign affairs, and discords and factions have full play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: collective management of executive authority often produces paralysis, conflicting counsel, and faction-driven decisions (e.g., unnecessary or ill-conducted wars). Institutional design should channel decision‑making to limit factional fragmentation in foreign affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation must be regulated by law, not left to arbiters
rubrics_metrics.description: This tax was regulated by a law made on purpose, and not left to the arbitrament of partial or interested persons; so that the more powerful citizens were in some measure restrained from oppressing the inferior sort, and influencing their votes in the councils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy criterion: equitable and legally grounded taxation restrains oligarchic coercion and vote‑buying. Anti-patterns include arbitrary collection, enforcement by rigour or violence, and using tax enforcement to suppress opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retroactive taxation (retrospects) is destabilizing
rubrics_metrics.description: The people demanded a retrospect, by which it might appear how much less the rich citizens had paid before... Giovanni represented to the people the bad consequences of retrospects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: retroactive accounting/taxation provokes long disputes and resentment; it may be exploited politically and can undermine social stability. Prefer forward‑looking, transparent fiscal rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party cohesion matters: compact parties prevail over divided ones
rubrics_metrics.description: If party is compact and entire... that very circumstance makes them so much superior to us... our party is divided, while that of our adversaries is compact and entire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic criterion for political strength: internal unity and cohesive leadership give a party strategic advantage. Anti-pattern: family and intra‑party divisions, envy, and pique weaken a faction's ability to defend positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political humility: accept bestowed shares of power to avoid envy
rubrics_metrics.description: If you would live with safety and comfort, be content with such a share in the government as your fellow-citizens confer upon you... it is that which a man arrogates to himself that makes him odious, and not what is voluntarily given him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative guidance for elites: seeking excessive or arrogated power increases personal exposure to resentment, exile, or persecution. Strategic moderation and generosity secure reputation and safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use different social groups seasonally (coalition management)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wise men always availed themselves of different sorts of people at different seasons; and if their fathers had made use of the assistance of the plebeians to humble the insolence of the grandees, now the latter were brought so low, and the former become so audacious, it would be no bad expedient to join with one to lower the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical political strategy: shifting coalitions are a legitimate tool to rebalance power between elites and commons; but this tactic can create enemies and long‑term instability if abused.
